1:
Neither Hebrew nor Chaldee gives this psalm a title, and Clarke notes that three of Kennicott's manuscripts join it to the psalm before; he reads the whole against the Babylonian captivity, with the oppressors of Nebuchadnezzar's empire as the proud. Delitzsch ties it instead to Psalms 92 and Psalms 93 by the anadiplosis all three share, and records the Septuagint inscription assigning it to the fourth day of the week — the Talmud preserves the tradition that the Levites sang it on Wednesdays, and the tractate Erachin the story that they were cut off in the middle of this very psalm when the Chaldeans broke in. Calvin looks nearer home: the persecutors are domestic foes rather than Gentiles, and he judges such intestine oppression more afflictive than open violence from without.

The opening line is a double vocative, and Ellicott renders it far more concisely than the English does — God of retributions, Jehovah, God of retributions, shine forth — marking emphatic repetition as a habit of the whole poem. Calvin reads the doubling as the faithful reminding God of the office that belongs to him: not because he needs admonishing, since he never resigns himself to indifference and his apparent delay is only his adjusting of the season, but because conceiving of him so emboldens them to pray with more vehemence. Spurgeon hears the same logic in shew thyself. The toleration of injustice is put down to the Lord's being hidden, and the bare sight of him will suffice to alarm the tyrants out of their oppression. He comes, he sees, he conquers.

On the claim itself the commentators are careful. Gill presses its exclusiveness: vengeance belongs to God and to him only, not to the gods of the heathen, not to Satan, not to private men; magistrates exercise it, but as his viceregents and no otherwise. Clarke is uneasy with the English word, since vengeance carries the sense of angry passion, where what the text asserts is retributive justice. Spurgeon guards the petitioner's motive from the same charge — a man could hardly appeal to God out of private revenge — and allows the prayer only as sympathy with right and pity for those made wrongfully to suffer.

Henry takes the verse as a solemn appeal lodged with the supreme judge, whose throne is the last resort, the dernier ressort, of oppressed innocency when the lower courts fail or are themselves the oppressor. Earthly magistrates do avenge, but under him and accountable to him. He adds that prayers of this kind are also prophecies: the righteous God will deal with the sons of violence according to their merits, so the petition already carries terror in it.

Why the psalm should be needed at all Augustine states plainly. It is known to everyone that men murmur at God's long-suffering, grieving that impious men live and have great power, that they oppress the good and exult while the good are humbled. Watching this, impatient and weak minds are perverted: imagining they live well in vain, some copy the wickedness they see flourishing, and others, restrained only by fear of the penal laws of the world rather than by love of justice, refrain from wicked deeds but not from wicked thoughts. Augustine warns his hearers that the psalm's mysteries are shut up not to be denied but to be opened to those who knock with piety and sincere heartfelt love.
2:
Lift up thyself summons God to the bench. Ellicott allows either be exalted or rise to give sentence; Spurgeon takes both at once — ascend the judgment-seat and be acknowledged ruler of men, and also raise thyself as a man does who means to strike with all his might. Render a reward he glosses as measure for measure, a fair retaliation on those who look down on the gracious poor and strike them from above. Gill hears in judge of the earth a title Abraham gave to Christ, and reads the petition as addressed to one whom his people apprehend as laid down asleep. Clarke identifies the proud as the Babylonians.

Two words in verses 3 and 4 carry the description of the oppressors. Delitzsch explains the first as speech that results from strong inward impulse and flows forth in rich abundance, and the thing spoken as unbridled and insolent. Over the second there is a real disagreement. Schultens took the verb to mean that they bear themselves as Emirs, and Ellicott reports the same connection with the Arabian title as the view of modern scholars: they make themselves out persons of distinction, or lord it over God's people. Delitzsch will not have it, since the Hebrew cognate means the top of a tree; the primary sense is to tower aloft, so the verb means to carry one's self high, to strut. Wesley catches the tone without etymology: to pour forth freely, as a fountain does.

Verses 5 and 6 turn from talk to blood. Ellicott renders the verb crush, comparing the grinding of the faces of the poor, and draws a conclusion from the victims: the stranger is named as one friendless under the tyranny of the great, which seems to imply that the grievance is domestic oppression, not foreign. Clarke reads the lines historically, of Nebuchadnezzar sparing neither age, sex, nor condition; Gill reads them of the church under anathemas, confiscations and cruel edicts, worn out as the saints of the most High. Their dispute over the referent runs through the psalm.

The atheism of verse 7 is what the psalmist attacks. Ellicott observes that the divine name here is Jah, and that this carelessness of heaven toward injustice, monstrous to Hebrew ears, was a settled doctrine elsewhere: he cites Seneca's Stoic god with neither heart nor head, the Homeric hymn to Demeter, and Tennyson's lotos-eaters careless of mankind. Clarke calls the saying either infidelity or insult, and suggests the Babylonians took Jehovah for the god of one province who knew nothing outside it. Spurgeon notes that the psalmist answers with the same verb they had used: they said God does not note, and now they are told to note. He calls them boors and swine, judges that the more such men know the more foolish they become, and would pity the scientific infidel rather than be humbled before him.

The argument from the body follows. Clarke marks its exact form: the psalmist asks not whether he who planted the ear has an ear, but whether he shall not hear, deliberately, to prevent our humanising God — Jerome's God is all eye because he sees all, all foot because he is everywhere. Wesley finds planted emphatic of the ear's structure. Ellicott hears in the next line, he who instructeth the nations, an anticipation of Paul on the divine education of the heathen; Clarke, finding no shall he not know in the original or the versions, would run the clause into verse 11 — Jehovah, who teacheth man knowledge, knoweth the devices of man, that they are vanity. Ellicott adds that the literal sense is for they are breath, referring not to the thoughts but to man collectively, though the Greek stands as the English does and Paul so quotes it. Wesley presses it home: he knows the most secret things, in particular your thoughts, much more your practices.
12:
The psalm turns, and Spurgeon hears a change of instrument: the mind grows quiet, the harp tuned to softer melodies. Henry describes the same move as looking above the instruments of trouble to the hand of God, which gives it another name and quite another colour. In verse 5 the enemies break the people in pieces; here God chastens them as a father the son he delights in, the persecutors being only the rod, howbeit they mean not so. Gill lists what the chastening is not — not of a cruel one, nor a magistrate, nor a master, but a father — and what it proves: a token of love, an evidence of sonship.

The blessing is not in the rod alone. Henry insists that it is not the chastening that does good but the teaching that goes with it and expounds it, and that the law is the best commentary on Providence; word and Spirit going along with its rebukes both mark a man blessed and help to make him so. Spurgeon puts it as a metallurgist: affliction without the word is a furnace for the metal, but no flux to aid the purifying. For Wesley, afflictions with divine instruction are true blessings. Clarke renders the verb whom thou instructest, and is careful about what God supplies — reason, revelation set before it, the Spirit to dispel the darkness sin has brought; but no new faculty, only the old one cleared and invigorated.

Rest follows, and its scope is disputed. Henry takes it generally: he that sends the trouble will send the rest, teaching his people by their troubles to prepare them for deliverance. Gill grants the respite God gives his churches in every age, but looks past it to a final one, after the slaying and rising of the witnesses. Clarke keeps it inward: the man God instructs has rest in his soul. Delitzsch reads the strophe as praise of the Lord as sole and trusty help. On verse 14 Clarke and Gill converge: the people are his inheritance, and whatever the withdrawal, he will not cast them off for ever.

Verse 15 draws the sharpest disagreement in the psalm. Gill takes it of what had seemed parted — God's government and his justice, hard to reconcile while the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper — coming openly together. Ellicott renders it for to righteousness judgment shall turn, and after it all upright in heart, the idiom of going after being the ordinary one for adherence to a cause, specially to Jehovah. To Luther's paraphrase, that Right must whatever happens remain Right, he prefers the older question whether the Lord of all the earth shall not do right. Clarke instead moves the vav to the other side of the shin, so the verb is not shall return but shall sit: until the just one sit in judgment, and after him all the upright in heart. The just one is Cyrus, who carries that epithet in Isaiah and appeared as the Jews' deliverer, the restored following in his train. Wesley keeps the plain sense: God will establish justice again, and the upright approve and imitate it.

Then the cry for a champion. Ellicott glosses rise up as standing forth to take the field, as Shammah the son of Agee did. Gill and Clarke read the church looking round and finding nobody to fight for her; Wesley makes it personal — I looked hither and thither, none appeared, and God alone helped me. Spurgeon finds the desertion useful, since a heart that could find friends elsewhere would hold its God less dear, and turns the verse on his century: error invades on every side, a false charity has enfeebled the valiant men of Israel, and one John Knox would be worth a mint. His consolation is that the God of Knox is still present and will call out his champions.
17:
Silence here means the grave. Ellicott points to the same usage in Psalm 31; the versions were blunter, as Clarke notes, the Vulgate reading in hell, the Greek in the invisible world. Spurgeon allows a second sense: either the psalmist would have died outright and gone into the silent land where no testimony can be borne, or he would have had no word against his enemies, wrapped in shame. Gill reads the extremity as the church's at the slaying of the witnesses. The next verse turns on one word. Clarke renders it propped me, a metaphor from shoring up anything falling, and describes the fall as a man got off his guard and then off his centre of gravity. Spurgeon insists on what the prop cannot be: nothing helps but mercy, no appeal being possible to any fancied merit — a thing true ten thousand times, he says, especially to the writer of the comment.

The multitude of thoughts is read three ways. Gill notes that the word is used of the thick entwined branches of a tree, and so of perplexed thoughts, which he catalogues: of God's majesty, of one's own sin as perhaps unpardonable, of the law by which one finds oneself carnal. Ellicott takes the root as dividing, and so anxious, comparing the Virgilian line about a mind cast this way and that, which Tennyson imitated. Clarke follows the Greek and Latin, which read griefs, the consolations answering to his sorrows. He adds that the verb for delight means literally to stroke, and so soothe, as a mother quiets her child, or as mourners are given the cup of consolation. Wesley identifies the comforts as God's promises and the memory of his care.

Verse 20 is the political question. Ellicott calls the throne of iniquity an apt name for an oppressive government and glosses the fellowship as association in it: could the theocracy admit to a share men who perverted justice to evil ends? Framing mischief by a law is making legislation a means of wrong, though others render it against the law. Delitzsch settles the verb's grammar, refusing the passive some read into it as a form for which no example exists. Spurgeon presses hardest: such thrones plead a right divine, but the claim is a fraud upon mankind and a blasphemy of heaven; they legalise robbery and then plead that it is the law of the land — and so indeed it may be. Righteousness is the one element a lasting order requires, and without it every such decree is wiped in time from the statute-book. Clarke and Wesley agree that God takes no part with unrighteous powers, and Gill hears the pretension of antichrist to be God's partner.

The gathering in verse 21 is judicial before it is violent. Ellicott suggests they crowd the courts to condemn the just, the Greek having them hunt him. Clarke observes that in everything evil such men are in unity, and applies the lines to Christ's trial. Spurgeon sees the popular party, unanimous in counsel and action, great at slander and not sticking at murder. Against them the closing verses set a rock. Clarke hears the natural fortifications common among the rocks of Judea; Spurgeon says the love is firm as the rock, and we ask no aid from man but flee into the bosom of omnipotence. On the last verse he observes that providence arranges retaliations as remarkable as they are just, wrath overtaking men while the stolen bread is in their mouths, so that faith reads the present in the light of the future and ends her song without a trembling note. Clarke, who has read the psalm against Babylon throughout, closes with the old Psalter: he sal yelde to thaim thair wickednes, and in thair malice he sall skater thaim. Gill adds the tradition that the Levites recited it at the fall of both temples.
